label: A Map of Open Frontiers
notes: This closing chapter spans printed pages 549 through 573 and is not a body of theorems but a catalogue of unsolved questions. We frame it as a map: name the objects, the known invariants, and the missing implication for each frontier, so students can navigate the research literature rather than memorise answers.

label: The Open-Problem Atlas
notes: The whole chapter is best held as one clustered graph. Eight problem families hang off shared methods: capacities, Floer theory, four-manifold invariants, and construction tools. Every cluster must connect to at least one earlier method node, which is exactly the invariant the notebook records when it builds this dependency atlas.

label: Existence and Classification of Structures
notes: The first frontier asks which closed manifolds admit a symplectic form and how to classify them up to deformation. In dimension four gauge-theoretic invariants constrain existence sharply, but in higher dimensions the deformation classification is wide open, and uniqueness fails in subtle ways already known from exotic examples.

label: Topology of Symplectomorphism Groups
notes: Here the object is an infinite-dimensional group rather than a manifold. We want the homotopy type of the symplectomorphism group and its Hamiltonian subgroup. Gromov computed these for the four-ball and some rational surfaces, yet for most manifolds even the connectedness of the symplectomorphism group remains genuinely unknown.

label: Lagrangians and the Nearby Conjecture
notes: Lagrangian submanifolds carry the deepest existence and uniqueness questions. The nearby Lagrangian conjecture predicts that every closed exact Lagrangian in a cotangent bundle is Hamiltonian isotopic to the zero section. Floer theory forces it to be a homotopy equivalence onto the base, but full isotopy is still open.

label: Fano Manifolds and Donaldson Hypersurfaces
notes: Fano manifolds supply a rich testing ground where algebraic geometry meets symplectic topology, and their symplectic uniqueness is largely conjectural. Donaldson hypersurfaces provide approximately holomorphic divisors Poincare dual to a large multiple of the symplectic class, turning a symplectic manifold into a Lefschetz pencil with controlled topology.

label: Contact Geometry and Fillings
notes: Contact manifolds are the odd-dimensional boundaries of symplectic ones. The open questions concern which contact structures arise as boundaries and how many symplectic fillings each admits. Tightness, overtwistedness, and the classification of fillings up to deformation drive much current research, especially in dimensions three and five.

label: Continuous Symplectic Topology
notes: This frontier asks how much symplectic rigidity survives under uniform limits. The Gromov-Eliashberg theorem says the symplectomorphism group is closed in the homeomorphism group, so symplecticity passes to continuous limits. Symplectic homeomorphisms, the Humiliere-Leclercq-Seyfaddine results, and C-zero capacity invariance are the live questions here.

label: Symplectic Embedding Problems
notes: Embedding questions ask when one domain symplectically embeds into another, a sharper test than volume alone. Gromov nonsqueezing already shows volume is not enough. Capacities give obstructions, and for ellipsoids into balls the answer is an intricate staircase function discovered by McDuff and Schlenk, still not fully understood.

label: Ball Packing and the Symplectic Camel
notes: The ellipsoid embedding capacity exposes a Fibonacci staircase of obstructions before settling to the volume bound. Ball-packing stability and packing numbers for projective space encode the same arithmetic. We illustrate the staircase so students see that the obstruction is combinatorial, not merely a smooth volume inequality.

label: Embeddings into Euclidean Space
notes: The final frontier asks which symplectic or contact manifolds embed into standard Euclidean or projective space with controlled codimension, and what flexibility Gromov's h-principle grants. Whitney-type bounds compete with rigidity phenomena, and the precise codimension at which flexibility takes over from rigidity is a recurring open theme.

label: Recap: How to Read an Open Problem
notes: We close by recasting the method itself. For any frontier, name the object, the transformation acting on it, and the invariant that should distinguish cases. The honest toy models in the notebook are scaffolds, not solutions; their job is to make each conjecture concrete enough to fail loudly when probed.
